title: Assignment Operators
subtopics: Difference between modifying a variable and modifying its object
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of assignment operators in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply assignment operators in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to difference between modifying a variable and modifying its object and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Assignment Operators through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding assignment operators helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Assignment Operators helps you reason about simple assignment. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Simple assignment. Then connect it to Compound assignment. The remaining syllabus points—Conditional assignment, Difference between modifying a variable and modifying its object—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports assignment operators. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain assignment operators, identify its place in data types, literals, and operators, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
